newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AWB as grains trader no challenge to Cargill - yet.
newsitem.headline: AWB as grains trader no challenge to Cargill - yet.

text.p: The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) is diversifying into international grains trading but does not see itself as challenging U.S. commodities giant Cargill in the trade, at least for the time being, chairman Trevor Flugge said.
Flugge told a Grains Leaders conference in Melbourne the AWB already traded Auatralian wheat to 40 to 50 countries and that this formed the basis for a successful commercial company.

"Any group of businessmen would love to get its hands on this," he said. He said the AWB would be embarking on an international grains trading programme in the next two to three years and haD every skill to be a very successful grains trader.
Saying he was "particularly bullish" about the AWB's prospects and "absolutely brilliant future", Flugge said that in the next 20-30 years it could be another Cargill. "It can be done," he said.
AWB general manager international Nigel Officer also told the conference that the group was well advanced in developing into international grains trading.

Already the AWB had truck optional origin deals with customers which provided for the supply of non-Australian grains in the event of drought or inability to supply grain of a specified type because of other constraints, he said.
The AWB faced the possibility of becoming a one-stop grain shop, Officer said.
However, international grains trading by the AWB would not get in the way of existing trading relationships, he said.
"We are not in the business of becoming the world's largest international grain trading company," he said.
"Where we see the opportunity to complement our business ... to identify the possibility of becoming a one-stop grain shop for our customers, that's what we are trying to do," he said.
"We are not going to knock Cargill off," Officer said.

The government-backed AWB, which has a "single desk" monopoly on the export of Australian wheat -- amounting to about 18 million tonnes from the last crop -- is facing privatisation by the end of the decade.
